query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The long‐term structural and chemical stability of near‐equiatomic, multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions is governed by the balance between high configurational entropy, which favors a homogeneous phase, and local lattice strain arising from atomic size mismatches, which promotes phase segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles with near-equiatomic composition and uniform elemental distribution fabricated by established physical or chemical methods.
generation.intervention: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles under identical conditions: a control set using elements with closely matched atomic radii (minimizing lattice strain) and an experimental set where a controlled fraction (e.g., 5-10%) of an element with a significantly larger atomic radius is introduced to amplify local lattice strain.
generation.conditions: Service conditions corresponding to catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric operation at 473–1923 K, in either oxidizing or inert atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions (strain fields) induced by atomic size mismatch within the solid-solution structure.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy in near-equiatomic alloys helps to suppress phase separation. However, if one element exhibits a significant atomic size mismatch, the induced lattice strain can overcome the entropic stabilization, accelerating atomic diffusion and promoting elemental segregation or phase separation under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature conditions, the control nanoparticles (with minimal lattice strain) will maintain a uniform, homogeneous structure, while nanoparticles with the introduced lattice strain (atomic size mismatch) will show observable phase segregation, selective surface elemental enrichment, or an onset of chemical inhomogeneities relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with elements that have closely matched atomic radii (and hence low lattice strain) maintaining uniform chemical and structural stability under the specified high-temperature regimes.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be significant primarily at elevated temperatures (773–1923 K). At lower temperatures, or with elements that have minimal atomic size differences, the impact of lattice strain on stability may be negligible.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative impact of atomic size mismatch on the rate of phase segregation and elemental diffusion is uncertain, as it may be influenced by additional factors such as specific diffusion coefficients and possible surface oxidation effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of near-equiatomic nanoparticles: one control group with elements having similar atomic sizes and an experimental group with a controlled addition (5-10%) of an element with a larger atomic radius. Expose both groups to high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions for a set duration. Characterize the post-treatment nanoparticles using in-situ or ex-situ high-resolution TEM, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess phase homogeneity and detect any segregation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental group (with induced lattice strain) does not show any statistically significant difference in phase segregation, elemental diffusion, or structural instability compared to the control group, then the hypothesis that lattice strain from atomic size mismatch is a governing factor for the stability under high-temperature conditions is falsified.
